## Worker Classification Review for a California Contractor

A careful review should focus on how the work was actually arranged and controlled, not just the title on the invoice or contract. The goal is to gather facts neutrally and preserve a clear record.

## Main Factors to Review

- **Control over work**: Who decided the schedule, methods, tools, and daily priorities?
- **Nature of the work**: Was the work part of the company’s usual business or a separate specialty?
- **Independence**: Could the person take other clients, hire helpers, or work without supervision?
- **Business setup**: Did they operate as an independent business with their own insurance, website, licenses, or business entity?
- **Payment structure**: Were they paid by project, milestone, or hourly like staff?
- **Work integration**: Did they use company email, systems, equipment, or appear on org charts?
- **Duration and regularity**: Was this a short, defined engagement or ongoing, recurring work?
- **Mutual understanding**: What did the written agreement say, and did actual practice match it?
- **California-specific test**: Review the relationship under California’s worker-classification rules, including the ABC test where applicable.
- **Tax and payroll treatment**: Were 1099s issued, or were payroll taxes, withholding, and benefits handled like an employee relationship?

## Documents to Gather

- Signed contract or statement of work
- Amendments, renewal emails, and scope-change approvals
- Invoices submitted by the worker
- Proof of payment records
- Time logs, schedules, or meeting calendars
- Emails or messages showing direction, supervision, or independence
- Deliverables, project plans, and acceptance records
- Evidence of who supplied tools, software, equipment, or workspace
- Business documents from the worker, if available: entity filings, W-9, insurance, license, website, marketing materials
- Any onboarding materials, policies, or access records
- Copies of 1099s, payroll records, or accounting entries
- Notes of interviews with managers or staff who worked with the person

## Clarification Email Template

Subject: Request for Clarification Regarding Engagement Details

Hello [Name],

Thank you for raising your concerns. We are reviewing the engagement from **2026-01-05 to 2026-03-20** and would like to confirm a few facts so we can better understand how the work was structured.

Please provide any information you believe is relevant regarding:
- How the work was assigned and managed
- Whether you set your own schedule and methods
- What tools, equipment, or systems you used
- Whether you worked for other clients during this period
- How you described your business relationship with us
- Any documents you believe support your position

We are gathering information to review the matter carefully and will consider your response as part of that process. This message is for clarification only and is not a statement of any conclusion.

Please send any supporting documents by [date].

Thank you,
[Name]
[Title]
[Company]

## Quick Actions

Action: [Button: Review Factors] https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/
Action: [Button: Check IRS Guidance] https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/independent-contractor-defined
Action: [Button: California ABC Test] https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/faq_independentcontractor.htm

## Sources

- California Labor Commissioner: https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/
- IRS Independent Contractor Guidance: https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/independent-contractor-defined
- California DLSE FAQ on Independent Contractors: https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/faq_independentcontractor.htm
